questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The energy base of the first industrial revolution
questions.learningObjective: identify why one fuel made mechanisation possible and scalable
questions.stem: The industrial revolution in one country began with machines driven by steam, and the fuel for those engines was coal dug a few dozen miles from the works rather than anything imported. Which feature of that combination does the most to explain the change?

options.text: Power taken from a fuel could be raised and sited anywhere, unlike a mill needing a stream
Coal was burned only in houses, and the machines were driven by something else
options.misconception: separates domestic heating from the power source of the new machines

options.text: The engines were driven by a river, and coal was burned only to move the water
options.misconception: replaces the fuel power with a site-bound water power that the change moved away from

options.text: The fuel had to be imported from a colony, so the change began outside the country
options.misconception: relocates the energy source to an imperial trade route the situation contradicts

questions.explanation: A mill on a stream or under a wind is married to one site and one power, and its output rises only with the flow, whereas a steam engine burns whatever coal is delivered and can be enlarged without moving, which is what let factories cluster where labour, coal transport and markets were best. The checkable feature is the siting freedom. The other answers detach the fuel from the machines, restore the water power the change displaced, or place the coal overseas.
questions.hint: Ask whether a windmill or a water mill can be moved to a better site.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the factory system did to labour
questions.learningObjective: describe the change from household-paced work to supervised wage labour
questions.stem: In a mill a worker arrived at an appointed hour, worked under a foreman for measured hours, was paid by the piece, and slept in company housing, whereas before the same work had been done at home at the household's own pace. Which change does that contrast describe most precisely?

options.text: Labour became supervised, timed and measured, so pace and output were set by the employer
Labour became better paid, since paying by the piece raised every worker's wage
options.misconception: assumes piece rates raise pay rather than output per hour

options.text: The household lost its workshop, but the family kept control of its own hours
options.misconception: keeps worker control of time, which the clock and the bell had removed

options.text: Skill became unnecessary, since the machines performed every part of the job
options.misconception: assumes full deskilling from mechanisation and ignores the new roles

questions.explanation: The decisive change is where the clock sits: work under a foreman in measured hours means the rate of work is set by the owner of the machines, and piece payment then makes the worker's own earnings depend on the pace imposed, which is the substance of the factory system rather than anything about the machine. The distractors each claim a gain, a retained control, or an abolished skill that the situation does not support.
questions.hint: Ask who decided how fast the work proceeded, and who bore the cost of a slow hour.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rulebook that measured work
questions.learningObjective: infer the purpose of factory discipline from a set of rules
questions.stem: A mill's rulebook of the 1830s fined a worker half an hour's pay for arriving late, required a foreman's signature for material taken out, and entered each worker's daily output in a column. Which feature of that rulebook tells the most about the change in work?

options.text: It made time and output recordable and chargeable, so the employer could measure what was taken out
It shows the mill preferred skilled workers, since the fines were set at a premium rate
options.misconception: reads a disciplinary scale as an apprenticeship or skill policy

options.text: It shows the workers set their own pace, since the book only records the day's output
options.misconception: treats recordkeeping as worker self-direction rather than oversight

options.text: It shows the mill owned its machinery, since the book names the foreman's powers
options.misconception: infers ownership of capital from a document about discipline

questions.explanation: Rules that can be enforced only where the employer can record what happened, and a book is exactly that, so the document's purpose is to make time and output countable and therefore chargeable, which is the administrative face of the factory system. The distractors each read a disciplinary instrument as an apprenticeship scheme, a grant of self-direction, or a statement about capital ownership, none of which the document addresses.
questions.hint: Ask what the rulebook enables the employer to do that the employer could not do before.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a railway joined together
questions.learningObjective: explain how a transport innovation integrates a distant market
questions.stem: A railway was laid from an inland coalfield to a port, and what had once travelled by wagon and barge between the two could now move in a fraction of the time for a fraction of the cost. Which change does that produce most directly?

options.text: A place that was remote and costly to reach becomes a short link from a port
The coalfield and the port become one market, so their prices must be equal
options.misconception: assumes a transport link equalises two prices by itself

options.text: Inland transport grows cheaper, so the port's shipping trade expands fastest
options.misconception: moves the benefit to a different industry from the one the line serves

options.text: Wagons and barges are made redundant, since the line carries every kind of load
options.misconception: claims one innovation retires the carriers it was built to supplement

questions.explanation: A railway does not make a place rich by being in a place; it works by shortening the distance between where a thing is produced and where it is bought, so a coalfield two hundred miles inland becomes able to supply a port and any market the port reaches, which is why output and railway building reinforced each other. The distractors each add a consequence, a compulsory price equality, or the disappearance of older carriers, that the line does not produce.
questions.hint: Ask what distance a buyer perceives, and how the line changes it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A mill moved to the railway
questions.learningObjective: read a relocation decision for the two economies at work
questions.stem: A manufacturer moved a mill from a riverside site to a town where coal arrived by rail, cut a siding from the line to the loading bay, and cut delivery time from a fortnight by canal to a day by rail. Which feature of that move is the significant one?

options.text: Power costs and freight both fell, so the site was chosen on two grounds at once
The canal on the old site had closed after a strike among the barge crews
options.misconception: invents a strike to account for a relocation the freight figures already explain

options.text: The town granted a rates exemption in exchange for building the siding
options.misconception: inserts a tax bargain the account nowhere mentions

options.text: Rail power left the mill independent of any supplier of fuel whatever
options.misconception: claims steam engines need no coal, which is the opposite of the case

questions.explanation: A mill's location is a calculation over two things, the price of the power that turns the machinery and the price of moving the output, and this move improved both at once, which is why siding access became a location factor in its own right and why rail towns grew. The distractors each reach for a cause the account does not contain, a strike, a rates bargain, or a fuel source the engines still depend on.
questions.hint: Ask what two prices a mill owner has to weigh before choosing a site.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The housing that urbanisation produced
questions.learningObjective: explain how housing design shaped a town's mortality record
questions.stem: As a manufacturing town doubled in twenty years, houses went up in back-to-back rows around a single open yard, privies were shared between neighbouring households, and cellars below ground level were occupied as rooms, while rents rose faster than wages. Which feature of that housing does the most to explain the town's mortality record?

options.text: Crowding with no drainage and no private water, so waste and drinking water shared the ground
The rows stood too close together, so the streets received too little daylight
options.misconception: reduces a sanitation problem to a lighting problem

options.text: The cellars were built for storage and were wrongly taken into use as rooms
options.misconception: treats cellar dwellings as an administrative mistake rather than a condition

options.text: Rents rose because too many houses were built at once, which should have lowered them
options.misconception: links higher rents to a surplus of housing, which would push them down

questions.explanation: The mortality pattern in such towns followed the water and the waste, and this housing design put both in the same place: a shared privy and an uncovered yard mean that what one household excretes is what the next household drinks, and a cellar room doubles the density of the exposed population. The distractors replace a waterborne mechanism with daylight, with a classification error, or with a supply argument that runs backwards.
questions.hint: Ask what the residents of a back-to-back row had in common with the water they drank.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A surveyor's account of dwellings
questions.learningObjective: read a housing survey for the sanitary conditions it records
questions.stem: A modern summary of a city surveyor's report on working-class districts records that a typical house had one room for a family of five, an earth privy shared with the house next door, and no drain, cesspit or piped supply, and that refuse was tipped into the street. Read that summary: what does the text establish?

options.text: The housing offered no way to remove or separate human waste from its inhabitants
The city's piped supply was contaminated at the treatment works upstream
options.misconception: moves the problem to a supply the summary says was absent entirely

options.text: The specific diseases suffered in those houses were named in the survey
options.misconception: supplies diagnostic findings that a housing survey does not give

options.text: The council had already refused to build sewers on grounds of cost
options.misconception: attributes a motive to a decision the summary does not report

questions.explanation: What the summary establishes is an absence, and an absence is exactly the finding: there is no drain, no cesspit, no piped water and a shared earth privy, so the arrangement leaves nothing between a household's waste and the next household's well. Each distractor supplies a fact the text withholds, a contaminated main, a diagnosis, or a recorded council decision.
questions.hint: Ask what the summary says is missing, rather than what it says happened.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A public health measure and its effect
questions.learningObjective: explain why an engineering measure cut disease before its cause was known
questions.stem: In a large city deaths from a waterborne disease fell steeply in the years after sewers were built to carry waste away from houses and mains were laid to bring clean water in, and the decline began before anyone in the city accepted that a germ caused the illness. Which feature of that programme best explains the result?

options.text: It broke the link between human waste and drinking water, which is the route the disease needed
It worked because the sewer crews wore clean clothing and mostly avoided falling ill
options.misconception: credits the workers instead of the engineering that changed the water supply

options.text: It worked because the disease happened to decline on its own over the same twenty years
options.misconception: attributes the fall to a natural decline rather than to a dated intervention

options.text: It worked because clean water made everyone stronger against every kind of illness
options.misconception: generalises from one waterborne route to all disease, which the record does not show

questions.explanation: A measure does not need a correct theory to work, and this one removed the route of transmission rather than the agent, so the deaths fell because a specific chain, waste, water, infection, was broken at one link whatever people believed about the chain's other end. The checkable feature is that the decline followed a dated engineering work and nothing else, which is what distinguishes the effect from coincidence.
questions.hint: Ask what the intervention changed, and what the disease needed in order to spread.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A doctor's note on one street
questions.learningObjective: read a practitioner's note for the strength of its claim
questions.stem: A modern summary of a physician's 1854 note records that deaths in one street were concentrated on one side of it, that households on the other side drawing from the same well were not affected, and that the local board of inquiry ordered the well's pump handle removed. Read that summary: what does the text establish?

options.text: A close link between one water supply and the deaths, and an action taken on that basis
A first proof of the cause of the disease, established by that inquiry
options.misconception: claims a causal proof that a local association does not supply

options.text: That every household in the street had already stopped drawing from the well
options.misconception: reverses who continued to use the well the deaths are associated with

options.text: That the board could order a water company to replace its pipes and mains
options.misconception: assigns a piped-water remedy to a note about a public pump

questions.explanation: The pattern on the ground is a strong association, concentrated on one side of a street, and the board acted on the association by removing the handle, which is evidence of a persuasive link rather than of a proof, since the note reports no test that would exclude other explanations. The distractors each claim a demonstration, a change in behaviour, or a power the board never had.
questions.hint: Ask how strong the claim is, and what the note does not say was ruled out.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A colonial economy built on one export
questions.learningObjective: explain why concentration in a single export creates vulnerability
questions.stem: A colony's export earnings came almost entirely from one raw material sold to a handful of buyers in Europe, the colonial administration took a share of the export price as revenue, and local farmers supplied the food. Which feature of that economy does the most to make it vulnerable?

options.text: When the world price of that one material falls, export income and government revenue fall together
Because only one material is exported, the colony cannot also feed its own people
options.misconception: assumes a single export rules out local agriculture, which the case provides

options.text: Because the buyers are so few, the price must already have been set by the colony
options.misconception: reverses bargaining power, since few buyers means a weak seller

options.text: Because revenue comes from exports, a price fall raises the rate to make up the gap
options.misconception: invents an automatic rise in the tax rate that offsets a price fall

questions.explanation: A single-export economy has one price and one revenue channel, so a fall in that price is passed straight through to the treasury, and a colonial state with fixed obligations and no reserves has no cushion, which is why such economies were so hard to defend. The distractors each misread the concentration, the direction of bargaining power, or the mechanical effect of a price fall on the tax rate.
questions.hint: Trace one price fall through both the export income and the government's books.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A colony's trade return
questions.learningObjective: read a trade return for what concentration it demonstrates
questions.stem: A colony's trade return for one year records that a single raw material accounted for well over four fifths of export value, that the top three destinations took more than half of the total, and that the government raised a tax rate in the same year to cover a revenue shortfall. Which reading of that return is right?

options.text: The concentration is visible in the figures, so a price or buyer shock hits exports and revenue together
The buyers fixed the price, since they took the larger share of the volume
options.misconception: infers price-setting power from the size of one destination's share

options.text: The colony traded with too few goods for a healthy national economy
options.misconception: judges diversification from a single year of returns without a comparison

options.text: The tax rise was already built into the export value recorded in the return
options.misconception: links two entries in the return that the document does not connect

questions.explanation: A return like this is evidence of structure rather than of a decision: four fifths of value in one commodity and half of it in three markets means the treasury's income depends on one price and a few buyers, and the revenue shortfall in the same year is consistent with that rather than a separate fact. The distractors each read a concentration as evidence of something the table does not show.
questions.hint: Ask what two numbers in the return would move together in a bad year.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a cash crop did to land use
questions.learningObjective: explain the land-use change a tree crop drove
questions.stem: A region gave up its fallow rotation and some of its food plots to plant tree crops for export, the trees taking fifteen years to bear, and the administration granted land only on condition that it be planted. Which change in land use does that produce most directly?

options.text: Land is committed to one crop for years before it pays, so fallow and food land are crowded out
Land is freed for food growing, since tree crops need no space between the rows
options.misconception: claims tree crops release land rather than occupy it for years

options.text: Farmers gain security, because a fifteen-year crop cannot be cancelled midway
options.misconception: reads a long gestation period as protection rather than as a risk

options.text: Yields on the remaining food plots rise, since fewer people now farm them
options.misconception: invents a labour effect on the remaining plots that the case does not state

questions.explanation: Tree crops tie a field up for more than a decade before any return, so a region converting land to them is trading a flexible rotation, which produces food and recovers fertility, for an inflexible one that produces an export and does not, and that is the land-use mechanism behind the shift in such regions. The other answers reverse the direction of the effect, or treat a long wait as a security rather than a constraint.
questions.hint: Ask how many years pass before the crop pays anything at all.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an oil concession was
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an exclusive commercial right from sovereignty
questions.stem: In 1908 a foreign state and a company signed an agreement giving the company the exclusive right to explore for and produce oil in Persia, together with a large share of the profits, while the Persian government kept its own laws, its own courts and its own taxes. Which feature of that agreement is the key one?

options.text: It transferred commercial rights for a term, not sovereignty, so the Persian state stayed in charge
It transferred sovereign authority, since exclusive rights cannot coexist with local rule
options.misconception: conflates an exclusive commercial right with jurisdiction over territory

options.text: It bound the Persian government not to sign a similar agreement with a rival
options.misconception: invents an exclusivity clause about other foreign companies

options.text: It made the company the lawmaker for the territory where it operated
options.misconception: turns a concession for extraction into a grant of legislative power

questions.explanation: A concession buys rights, and rights have terms: the company gets exclusivity and a share of revenue, and the state keeps the courts, the police and the law, which is precisely why oil was discovered in Persia in the first place, since the foreign interest had to be granted access by the local state rather than taken. The distractors each convert a commercial grant into sovereignty, an exclusion of rivals, or a legislative power.
questions.hint: Ask who still tried the company's staff when it broke the rules.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Concession terms read closely
questions.learningObjective: classify a concession from the powers it leaves with the state
questions.stem: A concession gave one company the sole right to produce oil in a province for sixty years, required the company to pay the government a share of the profits, and left the government free to pass its own laws, to tax the company's wages, and to try the company's staff in its own courts. Which reading of those terms is correct?

options.text: A commercial monopoly carrying rent, operated inside the state's own legal system
A foreign administration, since only the company was permitted to produce there
options.misconception: reads commercial exclusivity as territorial sovereignty

options.text: A treaty alliance, since the state's freedom to tax was set down in writing
options.misconception: turns a commercial contract into a mutual defence arrangement

options.text: A temporary import duty, since the state retains the power to tax wages
options.misconception: mistakes a power of general taxation for a trade measure

questions.explanation: The terms are legible in one line: the company holds the only production right and pays rent for it, and the state keeps lawmaking, taxation and jurisdiction, so what has been granted is an economic monopoly and not a piece of territory. The three distractors each need the state to have lost powers that the text says it kept.
questions.hint: Ask whether the state kept its courts, and what the company bought in exchange.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Coal smoke and a city's air
questions.learningObjective: identify which combustion caused an urban air pollution episode
questions.stem: In one capital the winter air was so polluted that lamps were cleaned during the day, a heavy fog repeatedly formed in cold weather, and visibility at street crossings fell to a few yards, and this followed the switch from wood and coke to coal in houses as well as in factories. Which combustion is most responsible for the degradation described?

options.text: Household coal burning, which put smoke into the open air across the whole city at once
Factory steam power, since one tall chimney damages more than a domestic fire
options.misconception: blames industry when the fuel shift in the case was mostly in houses

options.text: Street traffic, which raised dust through the cold months of the year
options.misconception: substitutes a dust mechanism for a combustion mechanism

options.text: Town gas lighting, which released a heavier pollutant than coal ever produced
options.misconception: credits gas with pollution that the case attributes to coal

questions.explanation: What makes a coal-smog episode a coal-smog episode is the scale of the emission and the weather that traps it, and when millions of households each burn coal in a grate, the total is larger than a handful of works, so the domestic hearth dominates even where industry is concentrated. The later clean-air response in such cities worked precisely because it changed what households burned, which is the checkable confirmation of the attribution.
questions.hint: Ask how many separate chimneys a city full of hearths amounts to.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A board of health's mortality return
questions.learningObjective: read a mortality comparison for the strength of its claim
questions.stem: A modern summary of a city board of health's return records that infant deaths in the districts nearest the largest factory chimneys were several times those in the districts with the least chimneys, that the difference persisted over two years, and that the board proposed limits on fuel burning in those districts. Read that summary: what does the text establish?

options.text: A persistent association between chimney density and infant deaths, and a remedy proposed
That smoke had been proved to be the only cause of the higher infant deaths
options.misconception: turns a two-year association into a proof of a single cause

options.text: That the districts with fewer chimneys were poorer and therefore had more deaths
options.misconception: supplies a competing explanation the summary nowhere offers

options.text: That the council had already adopted the limits the board recommended
options.misconception: converts a recommendation into an enacted measure

questions.explanation: The return establishes a difference that persisted rather than a single year's accident, which is a stronger claim than one number, and it pairs the difference with a proposed remedy, which is what a board of health was in a position to do. It does not establish that smoke was the cause, because the districts that differ in chimneys also differ in crowding, income and housing, and the summary reports no control for any of that.
questions.hint: Ask what a two-year difference shows, and what it still leaves unresolved.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a conservation act left out
questions.learningObjective: explain why a reservation without a duty was hard to keep
questions.stem: In 1872 a national government set aside a tract of high ground and hot springs as a public park, declared its natural features to be preserved from injury, left the land under the law of the surrounding territory, and created no staff, no rules and no penalty. Which feature of that act does the most to explain why protection was hard to keep?

options.text: The land was reserved without any legal duty to police it, so nothing followed a breach
The tract was too large to be surveyed before protection could usefully begin
options.misconception: blames survey work instead of the absence of a legal duty to enforce

options.text: The park was a state rather than a national park, so the centre had no power over it
options.misconception: attributes the gap to the level of government rather than to the missing duty

options.text: Visitors damaged the springs, and the act set out no rules for visitors at all
options.misconception: locates the cause in visitors instead of in the absence of enforcement

questions.explanation: Preservation is a legal duty and not a sentiment, and a statute that says a feature shall be preserved while creating nobody to check, nobody to fine, and no forum in which a complaint can be heard, has stated a purpose rather than created a mechanism, which is the exact defect that later conservation legislation had to repair. The distractors each supply a practical obstacle the act does not record.
questions.hint: Ask who would be fined, and in which court, if a feature were damaged.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A park act read as a mechanism
questions.learningObjective: assess a statute for whether it can be enforced
questions.stem: An 1872 act set aside a tract in a territory, required its natural features to be preserved from injury, placed it under federal authority for that purpose alone, and prescribed no penalty, no guard and no inspection. Which feature of that text best explains its limited effect?

options.text: It states a purpose and a duty but appoints nobody to enforce the duty
It left the tract in private ownership, so visitors became its only guardians
options.misconception: invents private ownership that the text does not mention

options.text: It set aside a fixed sum to pay for repairs to any damaged feature
options.misconception: supplies a funding clause the text does not contain

options.text: It required annual reports on the state of the springs, which were never filed
options.misconception: invents a reporting duty and its breach in the same breath

The three distractors each add an element, ownership, money, or reporting, that a reading of the text does not find.
questions.hint: Ask what a court would need in order to act on a breach of this duty.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An agreement with no mechanism behind it
questions.learningObjective: explain why a declaration without targets or enforcement cannot change policy
questions.stem: The 1972 conference on the human environment closed with a declaration of principles, a resolution for future action, and a plan for later meetings, and it set no binding target, created no body to receive reports, and prescribed no penalty. Which feature of that outcome best explains its small effect on national policy?

options.text: With no target, no reporter and no consequence, a government could sign and change nothing
The text was so wide in scope that no government could tell what it required
options.misconception: explains inaction by vagueness rather than by the missing mechanism

options.text: Member governments were prevented from legislating on environmental matters at all
options.misconception: invents a restriction on national legislation that the conference did not impose

options.text: The delegates were scientists who could not commit their governments to anything
options.misconception: assigns the failure to the delegates' standing rather than to the text

questions.explanation: A commitment becomes real when someone must report against it and suffers when the report is bad, and a declaration supplies neither, so participation costs a signature and nothing more, which is why a conference can be influential on language while leaving legislation untouched. The distractors each offer a different reason, vagueness, a legal bar, or the wrong delegates, none of which is what the absence of a mechanism means.
questions.hint: Ask what an unwritten commitment obliges a signatory to do next year.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A conference that produced only a declaration
questions.learningObjective: explain the difference between adopting a declaration and signing a treaty
questions.stem: At a 1972 meeting, governments adopted a declaration of shared principles, a list of recommendations, and a plan to convene again, but the meeting produced no instrument containing obligations, no requirement to report, and no body to receive reports. Which statement about that outcome is right?

options.text: Membership cost a signature, since a declaration cannot be breached as a treaty can
The recommendations were binding on every government that voted for them
options.misconception: treats a consensus vote in a declaration as a legal obligation

options.text: The plan to meet again shows the obligations were agreed and awaited signature
options.misconception: mistakes a future meeting for a finished negotiation

options.text: The recommendations bound the governments that adopted them without a treaty
options.misconception: assumes a document without terms can create obligations by adoption alone

questions.explanation: The difference between a declaration and a treaty is not how strongly the text feels but whether it creates anything to breach, and with no obligation, no reporting duty and no recipient for reports there is no act any government can perform or omit, so nothing follows from the signature. The distractors each look for a legal consequence in a document that deliberately contains none.
questions.hint: Ask what a government would be in breach of, if it ignored the recommendations.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The commitment mechanism of a climate treaty
questions.learningObjective: describe how a treaty secures pledges without fixing targets
questions.stem: The 1992 framework treaty on climate change requires each government to publish its own commitments, to account for what it has done, and to strengthen those commitments later, while fixing no percentage for any country. Which feature of that design does the most to explain why governments signed it at all?

options.text: A national commitment leaves the government its own target, so it can promise what it can do
A framework with no figure obliges every government to cut by the same amount
options.misconception: reads the absence of a common number as a common obligation

options.text: The duty to account lets other governments inspect any measure whenever they wish
options.misconception: promises open inspection that national reporting does not grant

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a demographic dividend closes
questions.learningObjective: explain why the same ratio that creates a dividend later reverses
questions.stem: Explain why the falling birth rate that opens a demographic dividend eventually closes it, and identify the stage at which the advantage turns.

answer.exemplar: A dividend is a ratio, and a ratio moves twice. When births fall, the cohort behind a large working-age population is small, so for a period each worker carries few children and few elderly, saving can rise without being consumed, and an economy can invest in roads, plant and training. The large cohort does not stay large, and when it reaches retirement age the small cohort behind it is the one paying, so the same ratio runs the other way, and it runs the other way quickly rather than slowly, because the number of contributors falls every year while the number of recipients rises. That is why a state which spends the whole window on current consumption, rather than on a pension reserve or on assets that pay out later, arrives at the second stage with nothing to cushion it. The same fertility history therefore produces both the opportunity and the problem, and what separates one country from another is not the birth rate but what was done while the ratio was favourable.
